claim: Lumbar dI2 spinal interneurons in chicks receive synaptic input from afferents.
source: We report that lumbar dI2 spinal interneurons in chicks receive synaptic input from afferents and premotor neurons.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating DRG neuron contacts on dI2 neurons.

claim: Lumbar dI2 spinal interneurons in chicks receive synaptic input from premotor neurons.
source: We report that lumbar dI2 spinal interneurons in chicks receive synaptic input from afferents and premotor neurons.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B-D demonstrating pre-MN contacts on dI2 neurons.

claim: dI2 interneurons innervate contralateral premotor networks in the lumbar spinal cord.
source: These interneurons innervate contralateral premotor networks in the lumbar and brachial spinal cord, and their ascending projections innervate the cerebellum.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating dI2 synapses on contralateral pre-MNs.

claim: dI2 interneurons innervate contralateral premotor networks in the brachial spinal cord.
source: These interneurons innervate contralateral premotor networks in the lumbar and brachial spinal cord, and their ascending projections innervate the cerebellum.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F demonstrating dI2 synapses on brachial pre-MNs.

claim: Ascending projections of dI2 neurons innervate the cerebellum.
source: These interneurons innervate contralateral premotor networks in the lumbar and brachial spinal cord, and their ascending projections innervate the cerebellum.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B-C demonstrating dI2 axons reaching the cerebellum and forming synapses in the granule layer.

claim: dI2 neurons function as interneurons in local lumbar circuits.
source: These findings suggest that dI2 neurons function as interneurons in local lumbar circuits, are involved in lumbo-brachial coupling, and that part of them deliver peripheral and intraspinal feedback to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity data showing dI2 neurons receive and provide synaptic connections within the lumbar spinal cord.

claim: dI2 neurons are involved in lumbo-brachial coupling.
source: These findings suggest that dI2 neurons function as interneurons in local lumbar circuits, are involved in lumbo-brachial coupling, and that part of them deliver peripheral and intraspinal feedback to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical data showing lumbar dI2 neurons project to and innervate brachial pre-MNs.

claim: Part of dI2 neurons deliver peripheral and intraspinal feedback to the cerebellum.
source: These findings suggest that dI2 neurons function as interneurons in local lumbar circuits, are involved in lumbo-brachial coupling, and that part of them deliver peripheral and intraspinal feedback to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity data showing dI2 neurons receive input from sensory afferents and pre-MNs and project to the cerebellum.

claim: Silencing of dI2 neurons leads to destabilized stepping in posthatching day 8 hatchlings.
source: Silencing of dI2 neurons leads to destabilized stepping in posthatching day 8 hatchlings, with occasional collapses, variable step profiles, and a wide-base walking gait, suggesting that dI2 neurons may contribute to the stabilization of the bipedal gait.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tetanus toxin silencing experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Silencing of dI2 neurons causes occasional collapses during stepping.
source: Silencing of dI2 neurons leads to destabilized stepping in posthatching day 8 hatchlings, with occasional collapses, variable step profiles, and a wide-base walking gait, suggesting that dI2 neurons may contribute to the stabilization of the bipedal gait.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating significantly increased collapse frequency in TeTX-treated chicks.

claim: Silencing of dI2 neurons causes variable step profiles.
source: Silencing of dI2 neurons leads to destabilized stepping in posthatching day 8 hatchlings, with occasional collapses, variable step profiles, and a wide-base walking gait, suggesting that dI2 neurons may contribute to the stabilization of the bipedal gait.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D-E and 7B-C demonstrating increased variability in knee height and TMP angle trajectories.

claim: Silencing of dI2 neurons causes a wide-base walking gait.
source: Silencing of dI2 neurons leads to destabilized stepping in posthatching day 8 hatchlings, with occasional collapses, variable step profiles, and a wide-base walking gait, suggesting that dI2 neurons may contribute to the stabilization of the bipedal gait.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2 demonstrating increased stride width in TeTX-treated chicks.

claim: dI2 neurons may contribute to the stabilization of the bipedal gait.
source: Silencing of dI2 neurons leads to destabilized stepping in posthatching day 8 hatchlings, with occasional collapses, variable step profiles, and a wide-base walking gait, suggesting that dI2 neurons may contribute to the stabilization of the bipedal gait.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral deficits observed when dI2 neurons are silenced.

claim: Interneurons that differentiate at the ventral progenitor domain, V3-V0, are involved in the control of rhythmic motor activity.
source: Interneurons (INs) that differentiate at the ventral progenitor domain, V3-V0, are involved in the control of rhythmic motor activity, alternating between the left and right limbs, as well as between the flexor and extensor muscles (Lai et al., 2016; Osseward and Pfaff, 2019; Alaynick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: V3-V0 interneurons are involved in alternating between the left and right limbs.
source: Interneurons (INs) that differentiate at the ventral progenitor domain, V3-V0, are involved in the control of rhythmic motor activity, alternating between the left and right limbs, as well as between the flexor and extensor muscles (Lai et al., 2016; Osseward and Pfaff, 2019; Alaynick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: V3-V0 interneurons are involved in alternating between flexor and extensor muscles.
source: Interneurons (INs) that differentiate at the ventral progenitor domain, V3-V0, are involved in the control of rhythmic motor activity, alternating between the left and right limbs, as well as between the flexor and extensor muscles (Lai et al., 2016; Osseward and Pfaff, 2019; Alaynick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some dorsally born INs (dI1, dI3, and dI6) migrate ventrally and are assembled within circuitries that control motor activity.
source: Some of the dorsally born INs, dI1, dI3, and dI6, migrate ventrally and are also assembled within circuitries that control motor activity (Yuengert et al., 2015; Bui et al., 2013; Andersson et al., 2012), while other dorsal progenitor neurons, dI4 and dI5, give rise to INs that mediate somatosensation (Lai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dorsal progenitor neurons dI4 and dI5 give rise to INs that mediate somatosensation.
source: Some of the dorsally born INs, dI1, dI3, and dI6, migrate ventrally and are also assembled within circuitries that control motor activity (Yuengert et al., 2015; Bui et al., 2013; Andersson et al., 2012), while other dorsal progenitor neurons, dI4 and dI5, give rise to INs that mediate somatosensation (Lai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: dI2 neurons originate in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: dI2 neurons originate in the dorsal spinal cord.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dI2 neuron development.

claim: The progenitor pdI2 cells are topographically positioned between the adjacent dorsally located dI1 and ventrally located dI3 neurons.
source: The progenitor pdI2 cells, topographically positioned between the adjacent dorsally located dI1 and ventrally located dI3 neurons, express Ngn1, Ngn2, Olig3, and Pax3 transcription factors (TFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dI2 progenitor cell positioning.

claim: Progenitor pdI2 cells express Ngn1, Ngn2, Olig3, and Pax3 transcription factors.
source: The progenitor pdI2 cells, topographically positioned between the adjacent dorsally located dI1 and ventrally located dI3 neurons, express Ngn1, Ngn2, Olig3, and Pax3 transcription factors (TFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dI2 progenitor cell molecular identity.

claim: Early postmitotic dI2 neurons undergo ventral migration.
source: Early postmitotic dI2 neurons undergo ventral migration and are defined by the combinatorial expression of Foxd3+/Lhx1+/Pou4f1+ TFs (Alaynick et al., 2011; Morikawa et al., 2009; Francius et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by data in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Early postmitotic dI2 neurons are defined by the combinatorial expression of Foxd3+/Lhx1+/Pou4f1+ TFs.
source: Early postmitotic dI2 neurons undergo ventral migration and are defined by the combinatorial expression of Foxd3+/Lhx1+/Pou4f1+ TFs (Alaynick et al., 2011; Morikawa et al., 2009; Francius et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the transcription factors Foxd3, Lhx1, or Pou4f1 is specific to dI2 neurons.
source: Importantly, none of these TFs is specific to dI2 neurons; rather, their combinatorial expression defines dI2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dI2 neuron molecular identity.

claim: The combinatorial expression of Foxd3, Lhx1, and Pou4f1 defines dI2 neurons.
source: Importantly, none of these TFs is specific to dI2 neurons; rather, their combinatorial expression defines dI2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dI2 neuron molecular identity.

claim: The lack of dI2-specific cell fate markers causes ambiguity regarding the molecular profile of late postmitotic dI2 neurons.
source: The lack of dI2-specific cell fate markers and the dynamic expression of the above TFs in other INs causes ambiguity regarding the molecular profile and outcome of late postmitotic dI2 neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lack of specific markers.

claim: The dynamic expression of dI2 TFs in other INs causes ambiguity regarding the outcome of late postmitotic dI2 neurons.
source: The lack of dI2-specific cell fate markers and the dynamic expression of the above TFs in other INs causes ambiguity regarding the molecular profile and outcome of late postmitotic dI2 neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the non-specific expression of markers.

claim: dI2 neurons are commissurally projecting neurons.
source: Using intersectional genetics, we have shown previously that dI2 neurons are commissurally projecting neurons (Avraham et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors and confirmed by data in Figure 1.

claim: The lack of dI2-specific TFs impeded their genetic targeting.
source: The lack of dI2-specific TFs impeded their genetic targeting.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lack of specific markers.

claim: Little is known about the wiring and physiological function of dI2 neurons.
source: Hence, little is known about the wiring and physiological function of dI2 neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The maintenance of stability and the coordination, precision, and timing of movements are regulated and modulated by the cerebellum.
source: The maintenance of stability and the coordination, precision, and timing of movements are regulated and modulated by the cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: Anatomical and electrophysiological studies of cats and rodents revealed two major pathways ascending from neurons in the lumbar spinal cord to the cerebellum: the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (DSCT) and ventral spinocerebellar tract (VSCT).
source: Anatomical and electrophysiological studies of cats and rodents revealed two major pathways ascending from neurons in the lumbar spinal cord to the cerebellum: the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (DSCT) and ventral spinocerebellar tract (VSCT).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spinocerebellar pathways.

claim: DSCT neurons are considered to relay mainly proprioceptive information.
source: DSCT neurons are considered to relay mainly proprioceptive information, while VSCT neurons are thought to relay internal spinal network information to the cerebellum along with proprioceptive data (Jankowska and Hammar, 2013; Spanne and Jörntell, 2013; Stecina et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VSCT neurons are thought to relay internal spinal network information to the cerebellum along with proprioceptive data.
source: DSCT neurons are considered to relay mainly proprioceptive information, while VSCT neurons are thought to relay internal spinal network information to the cerebellum along with proprioceptive data (Jankowska and Hammar, 2013; Spanne and Jörntell, 2013; Stecina et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Subpopulations of DSCT neurons are genetically accessible.
source: While subpopulations of DSCT neurons are genetically accessible (Hantman and Jessell, 2010), the genetic inaccessibility of VSCT neurons hinders efforts to reveal their actual contribution to the regulatory functions of the cerebellum in locomotion and other motor behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The genetic inaccessibility of VSCT neurons hinders efforts to reveal their actual contribution to the regulatory functions of the cerebellum in locomotion and other motor behaviors.
source: While subpopulations of DSCT neurons are genetically accessible (Hantman and Jessell, 2010), the genetic inaccessibility of VSCT neurons hinders efforts to reveal their actual contribution to the regulatory functions of the cerebellum in locomotion and other motor behaviors.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lack of genetic tools.

claim: The patterning of neurons within the spinal cord is conserved between mammals and birds.
source: The patterning of neurons within the spinal cord (Jessell, 2000) and the spinocerebellar tracts (Furue et al., 2010; Furue et al., 2011; Uehara et al., 2012) is conserved between mammals and birds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The spinocerebellar tracts are conserved between mammals and birds.
source: The patterning of neurons within the spinal cord (Jessell, 2000) and the spinocerebellar tracts (Furue et al., 2010; Furue et al., 2011; Uehara et al., 2012) is conserved between mammals and birds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chicks use bipedal locomotion that can be examined soon after hatching.
source: In addition, chicks use bipedal locomotion (evolved in humans and birds) that can be examined soon after hatching.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chick locomotion.

claim: Bipedal locomotion evolved in humans and birds.
source: In addition, chicks use bipedal locomotion (evolved in humans and birds) that can be examined soon after hatching.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolution of bipedalism.

claim: At E5, early postmitotic dI2 neurons migrate ventrally from the dorsolateral to the midlateral spinal cord.
source: At E5, early postmitotic dI2 neurons migrate ventrally from the dorsolateral to the midlateral spinal cord (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At E6, dI2 neurons assume a midlateral position along the dorsoventral axis.
source: As they migrate ventrally, at E6, dI2 neurons assume a midlateral position along the dorsoventral axis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At E17, 70.7% of dI2 neurons at the sciatic level occupy lamina VII.
source: Subsequently, dI2 neurons migrate medially, and at E17, comparable to postnatal day 4 (P4) of mice, most of them (70.7 and 71.5% at the sciatic and the crural levels, respectively) occupy lamina VII (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: At E17, 71.5% of dI2 neurons at the crural level occupy lamina VII.
source: Subsequently, dI2 neurons migrate medially, and at E17, comparable to postnatal day 4 (P4) of mice, most of them (70.7 and 71.5% at the sciatic and the crural levels, respectively) occupy lamina VII (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and F.

claim: E17 in chicks is comparable to postnatal day 4 (P4) of mice.
source: Subsequently, dI2 neurons migrate medially, and at E17, comparable to postnatal day 4 (P4) of mice, most of them (70.7 and 71.5% at the sciatic and the crural levels, respectively) occupy lamina VII (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This is a comparison of developmental stages between species.

claim: At all rostrocaudal levels and embryonic stages, dI2 axons cross the floor plate.
source: At all rostrocaudal levels and embryonic stages, dI2 axons cross the floor plate (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: After crossing the floor plate, dI2 axons extend rostrally for a few segments in the ventral funiculus.
source: After crossing, dI2 axons extend rostrally for a few segments in the ventral funiculus (VF) and subsequently turn into the lateral funiculus (LF) (Avraham et al., 2009; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and citation to previous work.

claim: dI2 axons subsequently turn into the lateral funiculus after extending in the ventral funiculus.
source: After crossing, dI2 axons extend rostrally for a few segments in the ventral funiculus (VF) and subsequently turn into the lateral funiculus (LF) (Avraham et al., 2009; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and citation to previous work.

claim: Collaterals originating from the crossed VF and LF tracts invade the contralateral spinal cord.
source: Collaterals originating from the crossed VF and LF tracts invade the contralateral spinal cord (Figure 1C and D; white arrows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: 73% of dI2 neurons at E17 are vGlut2+.
source: In situ hybridization on cross-sections of the E17 dI2::GFP-labeled lumbar spinal cord using the vGlut2 probe revealed that 73% were vGlut2+, while the VIAAT probe, which labels GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory neurons, measured 27% VIAAT+ dI2 neurons (Figure 1G–I; N = 308 neurons from two embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: 27% of dI2 neurons at E17 are VIAAT+.
source: In situ hybridization on cross-sections of the E17 dI2::GFP-labeled lumbar spinal cord using the vGlut2 probe revealed that 73% were vGlut2+, while the VIAAT probe, which labels GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory neurons, measured 27% VIAAT+ dI2 neurons (Figure 1G–I; N = 308 neurons from two embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The VIAAT probe labels GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory neurons.
source: In situ hybridization on cross-sections of the E17 dI2::GFP-labeled lumbar spinal cord using the vGlut2 probe revealed that 73% were vGlut2+, while the VIAAT probe, which labels GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory neurons, measured 27% VIAAT+ dI2 neurons (Figure 1G–I; N = 308 neurons from two embryos).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the VIAAT marker.

claim: At E13–17 at the caudal lumbar level and at the level of the sciatic plexus, most dI2 neurons are located in the medial aspect of lamina VII.
source: At E13–17 at the caudal lumbar level and at the level of the sciatic plexus, most dI2 neurons are located in the medial aspect of lamina VII.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Approximately 91% of dI2 neurons are small-diameter neurons located in the lateral dorsal aspect of lamina VII.
source: Approximately 91% of dI2 neurons are small-diameter neurons located in the lateral dorsal aspect of lamina VII, and 9% are large-diameter neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Approximately 9% of dI2 neurons are large-diameter neurons.
source: Approximately 91% of dI2 neurons are small-diameter neurons located in the lateral dorsal aspect of lamina VII, and 9% are large-diameter neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At the lumbar sciatic plexus level, large-diameter dI2 neurons are located mostly at the ventral aspect of lamina VII.
source: At the lumbar sciatic plexus level, large-diameter dI2 neurons are located mostly at the ventral aspect of lamina VII (Figure 1F) and at the level of the crural plexus in the ventral and dorsal aspect of lamina VII (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At the level of the crural plexus, large-diameter dI2 neurons are located in the ventral and dorsal aspect of lamina VII.
source: At the lumbar sciatic plexus level, large-diameter dI2 neurons are located mostly at the ventral aspect of lamina VII (Figure 1F) and at the level of the crural plexus in the ventral and dorsal aspect of lamina VII (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Large-diameter dI2 neurons were apparent only at the lumbar level.
source: Importantly, large-diameter dI2 neurons were apparent only at the lumbar level (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: dI2 neurons consist of several subpopulations.
source: Hence, dI2 neurons consist of several subpopulations, as has been shown in other spinal INs (Bikoff et al., 2016; Delile et al., 2019; Sweeney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the heterogeneity in size, location, and molecular markers, and supported by citations to similar findings in other interneuron populations.

claim: dI2 axons cross the spinal cord at the floor plate at the segmental level.
source: dI2 axons cross the spinal cord at the floor plate at the segmental level, ascend to the cerebellum, enter through the superior cerebellar peduncle, and cross back to the ipsilateral side of the cerebellum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: dI2 axons ascend to the cerebellum.
source: dI2 axons cross the spinal cord at the floor plate at the segmental level, ascend to the cerebellum, enter through the superior cerebellar peduncle, and cross back to the ipsilateral side of the cerebellum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: dI2 axons enter the cerebellum through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
source: dI2 axons cross the spinal cord at the floor plate at the segmental level, ascend to the cerebellum, enter through the superior cerebellar peduncle, and cross back to the ipsilateral side of the cerebellum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: dI2 axons cross back to the ipsilateral side of the cerebellum.
source: dI2 axons cross the spinal cord at the floor plate at the segmental level, ascend to the cerebellum, enter through the superior cerebellar peduncle, and cross back to the ipsilateral side of the cerebellum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Synaptic boutons of dI2 neurons were noticeable in the granule layer at the ipsilateral and contralateral sides of the anterior cerebellar lobules.
source: Synaptic boutons were noticeable in the granule layer at the ipsilateral and contralateral sides of the anterior cerebellar lobules (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Synaptic boutons of dI2 neurons were present in the central cerebellar nuclei.
source: Synaptic boutons were also present in the central cerebellar nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Large-diameter dI2 neurons were mostly colabeled with retrograde tracers from the cerebellum.
source: We found that large-diameter dI2 neurons were mostly colabeled, most of them in the ventral aspect of lamina VII (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Many of the cherry+ and LacZ+ precerebellar neurons were contacted by dI2 axons.
source: Interestingly, many of the cherry+ and LacZ+ neurons were contacted by dI2 axons (Figure 2F), suggesting that dI2 neurons innervate precerebellar neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: dI2 neurons innervate precerebellar neurons.
source: Interestingly, many of the cherry+ and LacZ+ neurons were contacted by dI2 axons (Figure 2F), suggesting that dI2 neurons innervate precerebellar neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of dI2 axons contacting precerebellar neurons.

claim: Segmental crossing at the lumbar level and recrossing back to the ipsilateral side at the cerebellum are characteristic of the VSCT projection pattern.
source: Segmental crossing at the lumbar level and recrossing back to the ipsilateral side at the cerebellum are characteristic of the VSCT projection pattern.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VSCT anatomy.

claim: 85 dI2 neurons were labeled at the lumbar level in the sparse labeling experiment.
source: 85 neurons were labeled at the lumbar level, 17 of which were large-diameter neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: 17 of the labeled dI2 neurons were large-diameter neurons.
source: 85 neurons were labeled at the lumbar level, 17 of which were large-diameter neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: The axons of all dI2 neurons cross the midline.
source: The axons of all dI2 neurons cross the midline.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: Longitudinally projecting dI2 axons were apparent at the contralateral VF and LF.
source: Longitudinally projecting axons were apparent at the contralateral VF and LF (Figure 3A–F; Video 1, Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3 and Videos 1-3.

claim: Axonal ramifications originating from collateral branching were apparent along the entire extent of the spinal cord.
source: In the gray matter, axonal ramifications originating from collateral branching were apparent along the entire extent of the spinal cord (Figure 3A–C; Video 1, Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3 and Videos 1-3.

claim: Bifurcation of the longitudinal dI2 axons was apparent.
source: Bifurcation of the longitudinal axons was also apparent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The bifurcating branch of dI2 axons elongated rostrally for a few segments and subsequently turned transversely into the spinal cord.
source: The bifurcating branch elongated rostrally for a few segments and subsequently turned transversely into the spinal cord (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 22 dI2 axons were counted at LS1.
source: We counted the numbers of longitudinally projecting axons at different levels (Figure 3A and D-H): 22 axons at LS1 (Figure 3D), 30 at T1 (Figure 3E), 21 at C9 (Figure 3F), 8 at the rostral brain stem (Figure 3G), and 7 entering the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 30 dI2 axons were counted at T1.
source: We counted the numbers of longitudinally projecting axons at different levels (Figure 3A and D-H): 22 axons at LS1 (Figure 3D), 30 at T1 (Figure 3E), 21 at C9 (Figure 3F), 8 at the rostral brain stem (Figure 3G), and 7 entering the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 21 dI2 axons were counted at C9.
source: We counted the numbers of longitudinally projecting axons at different levels (Figure 3A and D-H): 22 axons at LS1 (Figure 3D), 30 at T1 (Figure 3E), 21 at C9 (Figure 3F), 8 at the rostral brain stem (Figure 3G), and 7 entering the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 8 dI2 axons were counted at the rostral brain stem.
source: We counted the numbers of longitudinally projecting axons at different levels (Figure 3A and D-H): 22 axons at LS1 (Figure 3D), 30 at T1 (Figure 3E), 21 at C9 (Figure 3F), 8 at the rostral brain stem (Figure 3G), and 7 entering the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3G.

claim: 7 dI2 axons were counted entering the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
source: We counted the numbers of longitudinally projecting axons at different levels (Figure 3A and D-H): 22 axons at LS1 (Figure 3D), 30 at T1 (Figure 3E), 21 at C9 (Figure 3F), 8 at the rostral brain stem (Figure 3G), and 7 entering the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The elevated number of axons in T1 levels likely reflects longitudinal bifurcations.
source: The elevated number of axons in T1 levels likely reflects longitudinal bifurcations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of more axons at T1 than at adjacent levels.

claim: It is likely that additional dI2 axons enter the cerebellum at later stages of development.
source: Considering that the spinal cord was observed at E13, a relatively early stage of development, it is likely that additional axons enter the cerebellum at later stages of development.
evidence: This is speculated based on the early developmental stage of the analysis.

claim: Numerous collaterals of dI2 neurons that penetrate the spinal cord along its entire length were evident.
source: Numerous collaterals that penetrate the spinal cord along its entire length were evident.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: VSCT dI2 neurons projected to spinal targets at the lumbar, thoracic, and brachial spinal levels and to the brain stem and cerebellum.
source: Importantly, VSCT dI2 neurons projected to spinal targets at the lumbar, thoracic, and brachial spinal levels and to the brain stem and cerebellum (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: 10% of the VSCT axons belonged to dI2 neurons.
source: 10% of the VSCT axons belonged to dI2 neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The large-diameter dI2 neurons constitute 10% of the VSCT neurons.
source: Thus, the large-diameter dI2 neurons constitute 10% of the VSCT neurons, consistent with the anatomical observation that the VSCT comprises a heterogeneous population of INs (Jankowska and Hammar, 2013; Stecina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: The VSCT comprises a heterogeneous population of INs.
source: Thus, the large-diameter dI2 neurons constitute 10% of the VSCT neurons, consistent with the anatomical observation that the VSCT comprises a heterogeneous population of INs (Jankowska and Hammar, 2013; Stecina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Of 144 genetically labeled dI2 boutons, 121 (84%) were synaptotagmin-positive.
source: Of 144 genetically labeled boutons, 121 (84%) were syn+.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The synaptotagmin-negative boutons were significantly smaller than synaptotagmin-positive boutons.
source: The syn- boutons were significantly smaller (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Contact between DRG axons and dI2 neurons was mainly apparent in the dorsal dI2 neurons.
source: Contact between DRG axons and dI2 neurons was mainly apparent in the dorsal dI2 neurons, while the ventral dI2 neurons received little to no input from DRG neurons (2.8 ± 2.4 vs. 16.9 ± 11.3 contacts per neuron for ventral and dorsal dI2 neurons, respectively; p<1e-5; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Ventral dI2 neurons received little to no input from DRG neurons.
source: Contact between DRG axons and dI2 neurons was mainly apparent in the dorsal dI2 neurons, while the ventral dI2 neurons received little to no input from DRG neurons (2.8 ± 2.4 vs. 16.9 ± 11.3 contacts per neuron for ventral and dorsal dI2 neurons, respectively; p<1e-5; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Ventral dI2 neurons had 2.8 ± 2.4 contacts per neuron from DRG axons.
source: Contact between DRG axons and dI2 neurons was mainly apparent in the dorsal dI2 neurons, while the ventral dI2 neurons received little to no input from DRG neurons (2.8 ± 2.4 vs. 16.9 ± 11.3 contacts per neuron for ventral and dorsal dI2 neurons, respectively; p<1e-5; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Dorsal dI2 neurons had 16.9 ± 11.3 contacts per neuron from DRG axons.
source: Contact between DRG axons and dI2 neurons was mainly apparent in the dorsal dI2 neurons, while the ventral dI2 neurons received little to no input from DRG neurons (2.8 ± 2.4 vs. 16.9 ± 11.3 contacts per neuron for ventral and dorsal dI2 neurons, respectively; p<1e-5; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Large- and small-diameter dI2 neurons did not exhibit a significant difference in DRG axon contacts.
source: In contrast, large- and small-diameter dI2 neurons did not exhibit a significant difference in DRG axon contacts (10.4 ± 14.9 vs. 7.8 ± 5.7 contacts per neuron for large and small dI2 neurons, respectively; p=0.4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Serotonergic synapses were concentrated on motor neurons.
source: Serotonergic synapses were concentrated on motor neurons and were not observed on dI2 neurons (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3H.

claim: Serotonergic synapses were not observed on dI2 neurons.
source: Serotonergic synapses were concentrated on motor neurons and were not observed on dI2 neurons (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3H.

claim: The lack of synaptic serotonergic input may be related to the difference in species.
source: The lack of synaptic serotonergic input may be related to the difference in species or may suggest that other, non-dI2 VSCT neurons located adjacent to motoneurons are contacted by the reticulospinal neurons.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the lack of serotonergic input.

claim: The lack of synaptic serotonergic input may suggest that other, non-dI2 VSCT neurons located adjacent to motoneurons are contacted by the reticulospinal neurons.
source: The lack of synaptic serotonergic input may be related to the difference in species or may suggest that other, non-dI2 VSCT neurons located adjacent to motoneurons are contacted by the reticulospinal neurons.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the lack of serotonergic input.

claim: The analysis of synaptic inputs supports the concept that dI2 neurons constitute part of the VSCT.
source: The analysis of synaptic inputs supports the concept that dI2 neurons constitute part of the VSCT.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: dI2 cells receive input from sensory afferents and inhibitory and excitatory pre-MNs and project to the cerebellum.
source: These cells receive input from sensory afferents and inhibitory and excitatory pre-MNs and project to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The region innervated by dI2 collaterals overlaps with that of the V0 and V1 pre-MNs.
source: The region innervated by dI2 collaterals (arrow in Figure 5B) overlaps with that of the V0 and V1 pre-MNs (Lai et al., 2016; Griener et al., 2015) as well as with that of the contralateral dI2 neurons (Figures 1 and 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: The region innervated by dI2 collaterals overlaps with that of the contralateral dI2 neurons.
source: The region innervated by dI2 collaterals (arrow in Figure 5B) overlaps with that of the V0 and V1 pre-MNs (Lai et al., 2016; Griener et al., 2015) as well as with that of the contralateral dI2 neurons (Figures 1 and 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 5B.

claim: Labeling of dI2 synapses coupled with labeling of pre-MNs and dI2 neurons showed dI2 synaptic boutons on pre-MNs and dI2 neurons at the lumbar level.
source: Labeling of dI2 synapses coupled with labeling of the above neuronal population showed dI2 synaptic boutons on pre-MNs and dI2 neurons at the lumbar level (Figure 5C–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Synaptic boutons originating from lumbar-level dI2 neurons were apparent on dI2 neurons and on the contralateral and ipsilateral pre-MNs of the wings.
source: dI2 synapses overlapped with the putative targets, and synaptic boutons originating from lumbar-level dI2 neurons were apparent on dI2 neurons and on the contralateral and ipsilateral pre-MNs of the wings (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Lumbar dI2 neurons innervate the cerebellum, lumbar and brachial pre-MNs, and contralateral dI2 neurons.
source: Neuronal and synaptic labeling experiments showed that lumbar dI2 neurons innervate the cerebellum, lumbar and brachial pre-MNs, and contralateral dI2 neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 5, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: dI2 neurons may relay peripheral and intraspinal information to the cerebellum and to the contralateral lumbar and brachial motor control centers.
source: Hence, dI2 neurons may relay peripheral and intraspinal information to the cerebellum and to the contralateral lumbar and brachial motor control centers.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: All chicks were of comparable weight (average – 144.7 ± 12.1 g).
source: All chicks were of comparable weight (average – 144.7 ± 12.1 g; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: TeTX-manipulated chicks and control chicks maintained balance on the tilted surface up to 63–70°.
source: TeTX-manipulated chicks and control chicks maintained balance on the tilted surface up to 63–70°, with no apparent statistically significant differences (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Manipulation of dI2 neuronal activity did not impair the development or balance or muscle strength.
source: Thus, manipulation of dI2 neuronal activity did not impair the development or balance or muscle strength.
evidence: This is inferred from the weight and grip strength measurements.

claim: A 180° out-of-phase pattern was found during stepping in all the manipulated and control chicks.
source: A 180° out-of-phase pattern was found during stepping in all the manipulated and control chicks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Table 1.

claim: In control chicks, collapses occurred in 0.53% ± 0.92% of the steps.
source: In control chicks, collapses occurred in 0.53% ± 0.92% of the steps.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Table 3.

claim: In TeTX-manipulated chicks, collapses occurred in 19.46% ± 8.3% of the steps.
source: In TeTX-manipulated chicks, we observed collapses in 19.46% ± 8.3% of the steps, which was significantly different from the rate in controls (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Table 3.

claim: Most collapses (64.9% ± 19.7%) were not preceded or followed by overextension.
source: Most collapses (64.9% ± 19.7%) were not preceded or followed by overextension.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinematic analysis.

claim: About 22% of the collapses (22.47% ± 21.5% of collapses) were followed by overextension.
source: About 22% of the collapses (22.47% ± 21.5% of collapses, e.g., arrowhead in Figure 6C) were followed by overextension, suggesting a postcollapse compensation in the extensor drive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinematic analysis.

claim: Overextension following collapse suggests a postcollapse compensation in the extensor drive.
source: About 22% of the collapses (22.47% ± 21.5% of collapses, e.g., arrowhead in Figure 6C) were followed by overextension, suggesting a postcollapse compensation in the extensor drive.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of overextension following collapse.

claim: 12.63% ± 7.56% of collapses were preceded by overextension.
source: The rest of the collapses (12.63% ± 7.56%) were preceded by overextension.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kinematic analysis.

claim: A wide-base stance is typical of an unbalanced ataxic gait.
source: A wide-base stance is typical of an unbalanced ataxic gait.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ataxic gait characteristics.

claim: The mean stride in TeTX-manipulated chicks 1, 2, 4, and 5 was significantly wider than that in the control chicks.
source: The mean stride in TeTX-manipulated chicks 1, 2, 4, and 5 was significantly wider than that in the control chicks, while the width in TeTX3 was similar to that in the controls (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: The stride width in TeTX3 was similar to that in the controls.
source: The mean stride in TeTX-manipulated chicks 1, 2, 4, and 5 was significantly wider than that in the control chicks, while the width in TeTX3 was similar to that in the controls (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: The control group showed lower knee height range than the TeTX-treated group.
source: Further analyses revealed that, overall, the control group showed lower knee height and TMP angle ranges than the TeTX-treated group, even though there were differences within groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The control group showed lower TMP angle ranges than the TeTX-treated group.
source: Further analyses revealed that, overall, the control group showed lower knee height and TMP angle ranges than the TeTX-treated group, even though there were differences within groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average knee height range of the combined control chicks (1.981 ± 0.33) was significantly lower than the range of the combined TeTX-treated chicks (3.109 ± 0.74).
source: The average knee height range of the combined control chicks (1.981 ± 0.33) was significantly lower than the range of the combined TeTX-treated chicks (3.109 ± 0.74) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The average TMP angle of the control group (49.34 ± 16.03) was significantly lower than the average of the TeTX-treated chicks (77 ± 22.15).
source: A similar comparison of the combined ranges of angular excursions of the TMP joint during the normalized swing revealed that the average angle of the control group (49.34 ± 16.03) was significantly lower than the average of the TeTX-treated chicks (77 ± 22.15; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The significant difference between controls and the TeTX-treated chicks in the range of the knee height and the TMP angle excursions was maintained after excluding steps featuring whole-body collapses.
source: The data summarized in Table 3 show that the significant difference between controls and the TeTX-treated chicks in the range of the knee height and the TMP angle excursions was maintained.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: The increase in irregularity in the TeTX-treated chicks is not caused exclusively by the body collapses of the TeTX-treated chicks.
source: Thus, the increase in irregularity in the TeTX-treated chicks is not caused exclusively by the body collapses of the TeTX-treated chicks.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of increased variability after excluding collapse steps.

claim: No significant differences in landing angles were detected between manipulated and control chickens.
source: No significant differences in landing angles were detected (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The angles preceding a collapse were not smaller and even tended to be slightly larger than the landing angles that did not precede a collapse.
source: We found that the angles preceding a collapse were not smaller and even tended to be slightly larger than the landing angles that did not precede a collapse (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The increased frequency of collapses in the manipulated chickens did not stem from slipping and sliding events.
source: These results argue against the possibility that the increased frequency of collapses in the manipulated chickens stemmed from slipping and sliding events.
evidence: This is inferred from the landing angle analysis.

claim: The kinematic parameters of the dI2-TeTX-treated chicks demonstrate a reduction in stability during locomotion.
source: Overall, the kinematic parameters of the dI2-TeTX-treated chicks demonstrate a reduction in stability during locomotion, indicating a possible role of dI2 in the stabilization of bipedal stepping.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple kinematic deficits observed.

claim: The VSCT is thought to provide peripheral and intrinsic spinal information to the cerebellum to shape and update the output of spinal networks that execute motor behavior.
source: The VSCT is thought to provide peripheral and intrinsic spinal information to the cerebellum to shape and update the output of spinal networks that execute motor behavior.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VSCT function.

claim: The lack of genetic access to VSCT neurons hampers efforts to elucidate their role in locomotion.
source: The lack of genetic access to VSCT neurons hampers efforts to elucidate their role in locomotion.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lack of genetic tools.

claim: A subpopulation of dI2 neurons form part of the avian VSCT.
source: Hence, a subpopulation of dI2 neurons form part of the avian VSCT.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical and connectivity data.

claim: Lumbar dI2 neurons not only relay sensory and intrinsic spinal network information to the cerebellum but also act as active mediators of motor functions at the lumbar segments and at the wing-controlling brachial segments of the spinal cord.
source: We suggest that lumbar dI2 neurons not only relay sensory and intrinsic spinal network information to the cerebellum but also act as active mediators of motor functions at the lumbar segments and at the wing-controlling brachial segments of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity and functional data.

claim: One possible mechanism for impaired stepping following dI2 neuron silencing is that it perturbs the delivery of peripheral and intrinsic feedback to the cerebellum.
source: One of the possible mechanisms is that silencing dI2 neurons perturbs the delivery of peripheral and intrinsic feedback to the cerebellum, leading to unreliable updating of the motor output produced by the locomotor networks, thereby impairing bipedal stepping.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: Silencing dI2 neurons may lead to unreliable updating of the motor output produced by the locomotor networks.
source: One of the possible mechanisms is that silencing dI2 neurons perturbs the delivery of peripheral and intrinsic feedback to the cerebellum, leading to unreliable updating of the motor output produced by the locomotor networks, thereby impairing bipedal stepping.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: Mammalian VSCT neurons receive descending input from reticulospinal, rubrospinal, and vestibulospinal pathways.
source: Mammalian VSCT neurons receive descending input from reticulospinal, rubrospinal, and vestibulospinal pathways (Bras et al., 1988; Jankowska and Hammar, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons from the lateral vestibular nucleus have been reported to innervate extensor motoneurons at the lumbar level.
source: Neurons from the lateral vestibular nucleus have been reported to innervate extensor motoneurons at the lumbar level, as well as INs residing at medial lamina VII (Murray et al., 2018), the location where dI2 neurons were found to reside in our study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Neurons from the lateral vestibular nucleus innervate INs residing at medial lamina VII.
source: Neurons from the lateral vestibular nucleus have been reported to innervate extensor motoneurons at the lumbar level, as well as INs residing at medial lamina VII (Murray et al., 2018), the location where dI2 neurons were found to reside in our study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The vestibulospinal tract may convey input directly to the ipsilateral motor neurons and indirectly to contralateral motor neurons through dI2 neurons that innervate contralateral pre-MNs.
source: Thus, the vestibulospinal tract may convey input directly to the ipsilateral motor neurons and indirectly to contralateral motor neurons through dI2 neurons that innervate contralateral pre-MNs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: dI2 neurons may affect the motor output of the contralateral and ipsilateral sides of the cord by contacting commissural pre-MNs.
source: Thus, dI2 neurons may affect the motor output of the contralateral and ipsilateral sides of the cord by contacting commissural pre-MNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity data showing dI2 synapses on commissural pre-MNs.

claim: Specific targeting of dI2 subpopulations is necessary to determine the relative contribution of dI2 subpopulations to the impaired stepping phenotype.
source: Specific targeting of dI2 subpopulations – the precerebellar versus the propriospinal dI2 cells – is necessary to determine the relative contribution of dI2 subpopulations to the impaired stepping phenotype.
evidence: This is a logical inference about future experimental needs.

claim: There is no available genetic technique for differentially targeting the two dI2 subpopulations.
source: However, there is no available genetic technique for differentially targeting the two subpopulations.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of available tools.

claim: The precerebellar dI2 neurons also innervate the lumbar spinal cord.
source: In addition, the fact that the precerebellar dI2 neurons also innervate the lumbar spinal cord precludes the use of retrogradely target-derived neuronal activity modifiers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fact that precerebellar dI2 neurons innervate the lumbar spinal cord precludes the use of retrogradely target-derived neuronal activity modifiers.
source: In addition, the fact that the precerebellar dI2 neurons also innervate the lumbar spinal cord precludes the use of retrogradely target-derived neuronal activity modifiers.
evidence: This is a logical inference about experimental limitations.

claim: Early postmitotic dI2::GFP cells at E5 were a homogenous population defined by Foxd3+/Lhx1+/Pou4f1+/Pax2-.
source: The early postmitotic dI2::GFP cells at E5 were a homogenous population defined by Foxd3+/Lhx1+/Pou4f1+/Pax2- (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B, E.

claim: dI2 neurons that underwent ventral migration at E5, as well as at E6 and E14, express variable combinations of Lhx1, Pou4f1, and FoxP1/2/4.
source: dI2 neurons that underwent ventral migration at E5, as well as at E6 and E14, express variable combinations of Lhx1, Pou4f1, and FoxP1/2/4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: At E14, approximately 50% of dI2::GFP cells did not express any of the tested TFs.
source: At E14, approximately 50% of dI2::GFP cells did not express any of the tested TFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), suggesting that the early expression of TFs is required for cell fate acquisition, axon guidance, and target recognition, while their expression is not required after the establishment of the circuitry, as shown for other spinal INs (Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The early expression of TFs is required for cell fate acquisition, axon guidance, and target recognition, while their expression is not required after the establishment of the circuitry.
source: At E14, approximately 50% of dI2::GFP cells did not express any of the tested TFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), suggesting that the early expression of TFs is required for cell fate acquisition, axon guidance, and target recognition, while their expression is not required after the establishment of the circuitry, as shown for other spinal INs (Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of TF downregulation and supported by citation to similar findings in other interneurons.

claim: Approximately 12% of ventrally migrating dI2 neurons (from E5 to E14) expressed Pax2.
source: Interestingly, approximately 12% of ventrally migrating dI2 neurons (from E5 to E14) expressed Pax2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Pax2 is associated with a GABAergic inhibitory phenotype.
source: Pax2 is associated with a GABAergic inhibitory phenotype (Cheng et al., 2004), suggesting that a subpopulation of dI2 are inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A subpopulation of dI2 are inhibitory neurons.
source: Pax2 is associated with a GABAergic inhibitory phenotype (Cheng et al., 2004), suggesting that a subpopulation of dI2 are inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of Pax2 in some dI2 neurons.

claim: Similar percentages of Gad2- and Slc6a5-dI2-expressing cells were also found in mice.
source: Similar percentages of Gad2- and Slc6a5-dI2-expressing cells were also found in mice (Delile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The division of large- and small-diameter lumbar dI2 neurons was not reflected in the expression of the tested TFs.
source: The division of large- and small-diameter lumbar dI2 neurons was not reflected in the expression of the tested TFs or in a specific neurotransmitter phenotype; the inhibitory/excitatory ratios were 0.297 ± 0.13 and 0.343 ± 0.02, for large- and small-diameter dI2 neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The division of large- and small-diameter lumbar dI2 neurons was not reflected in a specific neurotransmitter phenotype.
source: The division of large- and small-diameter lumbar dI2 neurons was not reflected in the expression of the tested TFs or in a specific neurotransmitter phenotype; the inhibitory/excitatory ratios were 0.297 ± 0.13 and 0.343 ± 0.02, for large- and small-diameter dI2 neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The inhibitory/excitatory ratio for large-diameter dI2 neurons was 0.297 ± 0.13.
source: The division of large- and small-diameter lumbar dI2 neurons was not reflected in the expression of the tested TFs or in a specific neurotransmitter phenotype; the inhibitory/excitatory ratios were 0.297 ± 0.13 and 0.343 ± 0.02, for large- and small-diameter dI2 neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The inhibitory/excitatory ratio for small-diameter dI2 neurons was 0.343 ± 0.02.
source: The division of large- and small-diameter lumbar dI2 neurons was not reflected in the expression of the tested TFs or in a specific neurotransmitter phenotype; the inhibitory/excitatory ratios were 0.297 ± 0.13 and 0.343 ± 0.02, for large- and small-diameter dI2 neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: At E17, the stage in which the internal granule layer is formed in the chick cerebellum, the axons and synapses of dI2 neurons were studied.
source: At E17, the stage in which the internal granule layer is formed in the chick cerebellum, the axons and synapses of dI2 neurons were studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and timing.

claim: dI2 neurons, double labeled by genetic targeting and retrograde labeling from the cerebellum, are all VSCT neurons since dI2 neurons are commissural neurons.
source: However, dI2 neurons, double labeled by genetic targeting and retrograde labeling from the cerebellum, are all VSCT neurons since dI2 neurons are commissural neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the commissural nature of dI2 neurons and the double-crossing pattern of VSCT.

claim: Lumbar dI2 neurons may contribute to the inter-enlargement coupling described between the segments of the spinal cord that move the legs and the wings.
source: Moreover, the ascending axons of lumbar dI2 neurons give off gray matter collaterals innervating contralateral dI2 neurons and commissural and noncommissural pre-MNs throughout the brachial spinal cord (Figure 7D and E). Therefore, lumbar dI2 neurons may also contribute to the inter-enlargement coupling described between the segments of the spinal cord that move the legs and the wings (e.g., Valenzuela et al., 1990; Ruder et al., 2016 for forelimb to hindlimb coupling connectivity in mice).
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical connectivity and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lumbar dI2 neurons can provide the cerebellum and the contralateral pre-MNs with proprioceptive information, copies of motor commands delivered from the ipsilateral pre-MNs, and integrated information from contralateral dI2 neurons.
source: Thus, lumbar dI2 neurons can provide the cerebellum and the contralateral pre-MNs with proprioceptive information, copies of motor commands delivered from the ipsilateral pre-MNs, and integrated information from contralateral dI2 neurons (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is inferred from the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: A recent study suggested that dI2 neurons at early stages of development in mice (E9.5–E13.5, comparable to chick E4–8) can be divided into several subclasses based on their genetic signature and degree of maturation.
source: A recent study suggested that dI2 neurons at early stages of development in mice (E9.5–E13.5, comparable to chick E4–8) can be divided into several subclasses based on their genetic signature and degree of maturation (Delile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: E9.5–E13.5 in mice is comparable to chick E4–8.
source: A recent study suggested that dI2 neurons at early stages of development in mice (E9.5–E13.5, comparable to chick E4–8) can be divided into several subclasses based on their genetic signature and degree of maturation (Delile et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of developmental stages between species.

claim: Tract and propriospinal INs in the mouse spinal cord differ in the localization of their somata along the mediolateral axis.
source: Contrary to our findings, a recent study (Osseward et al., 2021) has shown that tract and propriospinal INs in the mouse spinal cord differ in the localization of their somata along the mediolateral axis and their transcription of TFs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Tract neurons reside in the lateral spinal cord and express group-N TFs.
source: Tract neurons reside in the lateral spinal cord and express group-N TFs, while propriospinal neurons settle at the medial spinal cord and express group-Z TFs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Propriospinal neurons settle at the medial spinal cord and express group-Z TFs.
source: Tract neurons reside in the lateral spinal cord and express group-N TFs, while propriospinal neurons settle at the medial spinal cord and express group-Z TFs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The analysis in mice excluded dI2 neurons.
source: The analysis in mice (Osseward et al., 2021) was applied to numerous cardinal populations of neurons but excluded dI2 neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: dI2 may represent an exception to the pattern where tract and propriospinal neurons differ in soma location and TF expression.
source: Hence, dI2 may represent an exception.
evidence: This is speculated based on the discrepancy between the current findings and previous literature.

claim: Precerebellar dI2 neurons share two wiring patterns: tract and propriospinal neurons.
source: In addition, our study revealed that precerebellar dI2 neurons share two wiring patterns: tract and propriospinal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-sheet microscopy shown in Figure 3.

claim: Applying single-cell RNA sequencing to dI2 neurons will reveal whether short- and long-range targeting in dI2 neurons are characterized by distinct transcriptomes or by a shared N + Z transcriptome.
source: Applying single-cell RNA sequencing to dI2 neurons will reveal whether short- and long-range targeting in dI2 neurons are characterized by distinct transcriptomes or by a shared N + Z transcriptome.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments.
